items.title: ❗️The United States (through Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner) proposed to Russia in late September three economic incentives in exchange for a partial ceasefire in the energy sector or at sea: the unfreezing of billions of dollars in frozen Russian assets (previously discussed up to $100 billion, possibly even before an agreement), the sale of part of Lukoil’s assets to a group of Middle Eastern investors, and permission for Belarus to export potash fertilizers. Ukraine, shocked by the scale of the concessions, set counter-conditions — the simultaneous allocation of equivalent sums to Kyiv and additional military aid in the event of a ceasefire violation. Negotiations reached a deadlock after Trump’s conversation with Putin and the announcement of the U.S. purchase of Russian diesel without any commitments from Russia regarding the war, after which the Kremlin stated that talks would not be resumed immediately, and the meeting in Miami ended without a breakthrough (NYT).

items.title: High-resolution satellite imagery confirms the vessel was berthed at Petersburg Oil Terminal’s PNT‑3 berth (59.88411, 30.16568) on September 22. The terminal handles a range of petroleum products, including diesel, jet fuel, heavy fuel oil and vacuum gasoil.
items.summary:
High-resolution satellite imagery confirms the vessel was berthed at Petersburg Oil Terminal’s PNT‑3 berth (59.88411, 30.16568) on September 22. The terminal handles a range of petroleum products, including diesel, jet fuel, heavy fuel oil and vacuum gasoil.
Michelle Wiese Bockmann (@Michellewb_)
Well that was quick. @Windwardai is already tracking what looks to be the first Russian diesel cargo sailing to the US east coast, due to arrive in ~48-72 hours.
Less than 24 hours ago OFAC issued General Licence No 135 that temporarily authorised the sale and import Russia’s diesel and gasoil until April 2027.
The MR tanker hasn't disclosed a destination since it sailed from the Russian Baltic port of St Petersburg last month laden with ~280,000 bbl diesel/gasoil ( @Vortexa ).
In reality, there isn’t much Russian diesel/gasoil to buy. There will likely be only a few cargoes that can be imported to the US right now. These are volumes that are unlikely to deal with the global shortage or meaningfully influence domestic prices in the US.
Russia’s diesel and gasoil exports cratered over the third quarter, falling to 190,000 bpd, Vortexa data show. That compares to 690,000 bpd in the second quarter and 850,000 bpd in the first.
Russia extended export bans on gasoline and diesel in July to address domestic shortfalls after attacks on their refineries over 2026 left 51% of capacity offline according to the Ukraine’s Defence Ministry as of Oct 4 .
Shortages were so acute the federation imported diesel/gasoil as well as gasoline over the third quarter. The most recent import was seen on Oct 7 with 150,000 barrels of diesel imported to the Russian port of Vysotsk on the Western-sanctioned Russia-flagged medium-range tanker Soyana (IMO 9327372) Vortexa data show.
The six-month licence also suggests, that as per my earlier posts, nobody sees freedom of navigation being restored to the Strait of Hormuz any time soon.
— http://nitter.pp.ua/Michellewb_/status/2108868957096513564#m

The diffusion of drone technology and tactics will increase, particularly whenever the Russo-Ukraine war ends. I doubt that we are prepared.
items.summary:
In Latin America, Africa, and the Middle East, we are seeing early drone warfare. I would equate this to where Ukraine and Russia were in 2023. The diffusion of drone technology and tactics will increase, particularly whenever the Russo-Ukraine war ends. I doubt that we are prepared.
Ryan O'Leary (@RyanO_ChosenCoy)
One thing that is becoming more common is “PMC” type and drone companies hiring foreigners who did drones in Ukraine for work. The main problem with that, is that anyone can learn to fly a drone in 14-21 days. Give them 6 weeks and they’ll be hitting targets. What they don’t learn in-depth typically is the tactics behind drones (especially for the 6 monthers) or get a good grasp on signals/frequency and all the overly nerdy shit involved in that realm.
Not understanding frequencies and drone tactics in general will create a lot of scenarios such as this as outside of the Ukrainian war, front areas are not saturated with signals and hundreds of drones flying around so it’s much more easy to pinpoint launch positions and also signal locations.

items.title: RT by @DefMon3: "The first word brigade and corps commanders use to describe the first few months of Drapatyi's tenure is 'freedom'. Unlike his predecessor, who would tell some brigade commanders how and where to fight – even specifying the coordinates where a position should be set up – Drapatyi has chosen a different approach. He has opted to decentralize command, moving away from the 'micromanagement' that has already become widely known to the public... Ukrainska Pravda sources say the move away from hands-on management of brigades and corps has brought another change: Drapatyi no longer spends several hours every day hearing reports from all commanders, as Syrskyi did. 'Syrskyi would hear reports from everyone every day and could give specific instructions on how to respond to developments, including where troops should advance… Drapatyi doesn't do that; that's the job of the troop grouping commanders. Drapatyi focuses on strategic and systemic issues. And when commanders do speak to the commander-in-chief, he isn't interested in a standard report on 'what happened', but in statistics, analysing problems and finding solutions – in other words, what conditions need to be created for a particular commander to accomplish their mission. And that's the right approach,' a senior military officer told Ukrainska Pravda." https://www.pravda.com.ua/eng/news/2026/10/05/8056518/
